Hypothetical

/hy-puh-THET-ih-kul/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Hypothetical means supposed or assumed to be true for the sake of argument, but unproven

Hypothetical means supposed or assumed to be true for the sake of argument, but unproven

Worked Example

The coach sketched a <strong style="color:var(--accent);">hypothetical</strong> ending on the whiteboard — 'suppose we're down two points with ten seconds left' — so the team could rehearse its response.

The situation is invented and assumed for practice: the team isn't actually down two points. An imagined 'suppose' scenario is the hallmark of something hypothetical.

How Hypothetical Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

theoretical

theoretical: existing in theory rather than practice

supposed

supposed: assumed to be so

imagined

imagined: formed in the mind, not real

Antonyms

actual

actual: existing in fact

proven

proven: shown to be true

How Strong Is It? — possible → hypothetical → fanciful

possible vs. hypothetical

possible vs. hypothetical: Possible is milder than hypothetical — a possible outcome might really happen, while a hypothetical one is deliberately assumed just for the sake of discussion.

fanciful vs. hypothetical

fanciful vs. hypothetical: Fanciful goes further than hypothetical — a hypothetical scenario is at least built for serious reasoning, but a fanciful one floats free of reality altogether.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — hypo-

Prefix — hypo-: under, beneath (Greek)

Root — thet-

Root — thet-: placed, put (Greek tithenai, to place)

Suffix — -ical

Suffix — -ical: relating to

Put it together

Put it together: A hypothesis is literally 'a placing under' — a foundation set beneath an argument for the sake of discussion. Hypothetical describes any idea resting on that supposed, not-yet-proven foundation.

Use the root in a new word: antithesis

Use the root in a new word: antithesis: Her calm, careful driving was the antithesis of her brother's reckless speeding — the two placed at opposite poles.

Word Choice

Academic and everyday

A hypothetical question or scenario is posed 'for the sake of argument' — you'll hear it in classrooms, interviews, and courtrooms alike. Keep it distinct from empirical, a word from this same unit: hypothetical claims are assumed without proof, while empirical claims rest on observed evidence. They describe opposite ways of supporting an idea.
